question: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology share 90 % of the random access memory (RAM) market. RAM is a key component of our digital devices, but these three companies have, simultaneously, cut back the supply to the general public (computers, video game consoles, phones, etc.) in order to supply AI data centres.

As a result, RAM is now as expensive as it was in 2010 – sixteen years of falling prices wiped out in a matter of months. And these giants know that the cost of entering the market is so high that there will be no competitors to put an end to the skyrocketing prices. In the meantime, it is Europeans who are bearing the cost.

Computer manufacturers are announcing a 15 to 20 % price jump and Sony has increased the cost of its PS5 by EUR 100. As for the three manufactures, they are all making record profits. However, the trio had already been sanctioned by the Commission in 2010 for colluding on prices and creating a cartel. On 25 June 2026, a new lawsuit involving the same allegations was brought against them in the United States.
Under its antitrust rules, does the Commission intend to launch a sector inquiry into these companies and, if necessary, take legal action against them?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The Commission is aware of the market developments referred to by the Honourable Member in the memory chip sector. The Commission takes possible infringements of EU competition rules seriously and has previously taken enforcement action in the semiconductor sector, including against a cartel involving producers of dynamic random access memory chips.
Under Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 1/20031, the Commission may conduct a sector inquiry where market developments suggest that competition may be restricted or distorted.

The decision whether to launch such an inquiry or to investigate potential infringements of Articles 101 or 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union depends on the circumstances of the case, the information available and the Commission's enforcement priorities.
The Commission continues to monitor market developments in this sector and stands ready to take appropriate enforcement action where warranted.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2003 of 16 December 2002 on the implementation of the rules on competition
laid down in Articles 81 and 82 of the Treaty.
